questions: What piles up under the curve as x sweeps right?
Why is the antiderivative described as accumulated area?
segments.say: Integration undoes differentiation - but picture it as area. Watch the sweep dot travel right along the curve and the shaded strips pile up behind it. The antiderivative at each point is exactly that accumulated area. Tell your partner: what is accumulating, and where?

questions: Why do thinner rectangles give a better estimate?
What does the Riemann sum become in the limit?
segments.say: Now measure that area with rectangles. Four wide rectangles give a rough total; eight narrower ones get closer. Keep halving the widths and the sum converges on the exact shaded area - that limit is the definite integral, a Riemann sum taken to the limit.

questions: Why do we subtract the lower bound value?
segments.say: Evaluate one exactly. Integrate 2x from 1 to 2: antidifferentiate to x^2, evaluate at the bounds - 4 at x = 2, 1 at x = 1 - and subtract: 4 - 1 = 3 square units. Three moves every time: antidifferentiate, evaluate, subtract.

questions: Differentiate x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 - what do you get both times?
Why does the indefinite integral need +C?
segments.say: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: it is tempting to write the integral of 2x as just x^2. But look at the shifted curves - x^2 + 5 and x^2 - 3 have exactly the same slope, 2x, everywhere. One derivative, a whole family of antiderivatives, and the +C is how we name them all.

questions: What must every indefinite integral include?
What are the three moves for a definite integral?
segments.say: Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each indefinite integral against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: definite means antidifferentiate, evaluate, subtract; indefinite means never drop the +C.
segments.watchFor: The integral of 2x is x^2. Listen for students who write x^2 with no +C on any indefinite integral. Send them back to the shifted curves: Never drop the +C: differentiating x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 both give 2x.
